title: 3-Read Friday #80: Lethal Mutations, Career Habits, and Direct Instruction
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #80 gathers three posts on getting research, career habits, and instructional models right in practice rather than in theory. Haili Hughes examines how well-evidenced principles - interleaving, growth mindset, retrieval practice - routinely mutate into ineffective or even harmful classroom versions once schools attempt to implement them at scale, and sets out what leaders can do to keep the underlying research intact. Nimish Lad takes a more personal, career-focused turn, naming six quiet habits - avoiding difficult conversations, downplaying one's own work, perfectionism, over-committing, clinging to routine, and avoiding self-promotion - that erode professional growth over time, alongside a specific reframe for shifting each one. Dylan Kane, continuing his engagement with Direct Instruction from a year prior, reports that while he remains uninterested in becoming a full Direct Instruction teacher, he has adopted three concrete DI-derived practices into his own maths classroom: choral response, short spaced chunks of practice spread across many lessons, and deliberately building in review of prerequisite skills before starting a new unit. Barton's editorial thread across the issue: taking research or a proven model seriously means engaging with its substance and adapting selectively, not adopting it wholesale or letting it degrade through careless implementation.
points: Haili Hughes's core argument: well-evidenced principles like interleaving, growth mindset, and retrieval practice routinely 'lethally mutate' into distorted, less effective classroom versions once schools try to implement them at scale, and school leaders bear responsibility for keeping the underlying research intact during rollout.

Nimish Lad's six career-limiting habits: dodging difficult conversations, downplaying one's own work, perfectionism disguised as high standards, over-committing ('yes' when you mean 'I'm overwhelmed'), clinging to familiar routines, and avoiding self-promotion entirely.
Lad frames each habit's fix as a specific reframe rather than a willpower fix - e.g., treating self-promotion as storytelling, or embracing a 'working draft' mindset to counter perfectionism.

Dylan Kane's three Direct Instruction-derived practices he has kept, despite rejecting DI as a whole-school system: choral response for quick, low-prep checks for understanding; spreading practice across many short chunks over weeks rather than one intensive block; and explicitly pre-teaching prerequisite skills before a new unit begins.

Kane reports that a typical Direct Instruction lesson spends 80-90% of its time on practice and review of previously-introduced material rather than new content - a ratio he uses as an aspirational benchmark even though he doesn't fully adopt DI's whole-school structure.
quotes: Hali examines how potentially effective principles from research have been misapplied in schools -- such as interleaving, growth mindset, and retrieval practice -- and what schools can do about it.
Nimish examines six habits he has seen hold back himself or his colleagues, and suggests strategies to overcome them. How many can you relate to?
Dylan took a deep dive into the Direct Instruction world, concluded that it was not for him, but found three principles that he has taken forward into his teaching. A great read!
